## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
```

```{r}
ems_train <- read_csv(
  "../data/processed/ems_train.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE)

ems_test <- read_csv(
  "../data/processed/ems_test.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(ems_train)
glimpse(ems_test)
```

## Prepare Weekly Demand Series

The forecasting analysis focuses on three views of EMS demand: total weekly incidents, life-threatening incidents, and non-life-threatening incidents. This allows the overall demand forecast to be compared with the two emergency categories.

Total weekly EMS demand is calculated by summing life-threatening and non-life-threatening incidents. The 23 unclassified incidents identified during data cleaning are excluded to maintain consistency with the category-level analysis.

```{r}
category_train <- ems_train |>
  select(Week, Category, Incidents) |>
  as_tsibble(key = Category, index = Week)

category_test <- ems_test |>
  select(Week, Category, Incidents) |>
  as_tsibble(key = Category, index = Week)

total_train <- ems_train |>
  group_by(Week) |>
  summarise(Incidents = sum(Incidents), .groups = "drop") |>
  as_tsibble(index = Week)

total_test <- ems_test |>
  group_by(Week) |>
  summarise(Incidents = sum(Incidents), .groups = "drop") |>
  as_tsibble(index = Week)
```

```{r}
category_train |>
  autoplot(Incidents) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly NYC EMS Demand by Emergency Category",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Incidents",
    color = "Category")
```

The two emergency categories follow many of the same broad changes over time, but their weekly volumes and variability differ. Forecasting the categories separately makes it possible to evaluate whether one type of EMS demand is more predictable than the other.

## Initial ARIMA Analysis: Non-Life-Threatening Demand

The initial ARIMA analysis focused on non-life threatening incidents. This section is retained because it provides a detailed comparison of candidate ARIMA specifications before expanding the analysis to total demand and both emergency categories.

```{r}
ntl_train <- category_train |>
  filter(Category == "Non-Life-Threatening") |>
  select(Week, Incidents)

ntl_test <- category_test |>
  filter(Category == "Non-Life-Threatening") |>
  select(Week, Incidents)
```

```{r}
ntl_train |>
  autoplot(Incidents) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly Non-Life-Threatening EMS Incidents",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Incidents")
```

```{r}
ntl_train |>
  features(Incidents, unitroot_ndiffs)

ntl_train |>
  features(Incidents, unitroot_nsdiffs)
```

```{r}
ntl_train |>
  mutate(
    diff_incidents = difference(Incidents)
  ) |>
  gg_tsdisplay(
    diff_incidents,
    plot_type = "partial")
```

The differencing tests suggested one regular difference and no seasonal difference. After differencing, the strongest ACF and PACF relationships appeared at the first lag, so I compared simple ARIMA(1,1,0) and ARIMA(0,1,1) models with an automatically selected ARIMA model.

```{r}
manual_fit <- ntl_train |>
  model(
    AR1 = ARIMA(Incidents ~ pdq(1, 1, 0)),
    MA1 = ARIMA(Incidents ~ pdq(0, 1, 1)),
    Auto = ARIMA(Incidents))
```

```{r}
glance(manual_fit) |>
  select(.model, AIC, AICc, BIC) |>
  arrange(AICc)
```

```{r}
ntl_fc <- manual_fit |>
  forecast(new_data = ntl_test)

ntl_accuracy <- accuracy(ntl_fc, ntl_test) |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(RMSE)

ntl_accuracy
```

```{r}
ntl_fc |>
  autoplot(
    ntl_train |> filter_index("2023 Jan" ~ .),
    level = NULL
  ) +
  autolayer(
    ntl_test,
    Incidents
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Non-Life-Threatening EMS Demand: Actual vs. Forecast",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Incidents")
```

```{r}
manual_fit |>
  select(MA1) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

The residuals are generally centered around zero, with most autocorrelations remaining within the significance bounds. There are a few larger residuals, especially around 2020, which likely reflect unusual changes in EMS demand during that period. Overall, the residual diagnostics do not show a strong remaining pattern, so the ARIMA (0,1,1) model appears reasonable for forecasting.

The ARIMA (0,1,1) model performed best on the test data, with an RMSE of 714.8, MAE of 644.5, and MAPE of 5.61%. Although the automatically selected ARIMA (2,1,2) model had the lowest AICc on the training data, it performed worse during the test period. For this holdout period, the simpler model provided better forecasts on new data.

## Total Weekly EMS Demand: ARIMA vs. ETS

To address the broader project objective, I next modeled total weekly EMS incidents. ARIMA and ETS were compared so the analysis was not limited to a single model family.

```{r}
total_fit <- total_train |>
  model(
    ARIMA = ARIMA(Incidents),
    ETS = ETS(Incidents))

total_fit
```

```{r}
total_fc <- total_fit |>
  forecast(new_data = total_test)

total_accuracy <- accuracy(total_fc, total_test) |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(RMSE)

total_accuracy
```

```{r}
total_fc |>
  autoplot(
    total_train |> filter_index("2023 Jan" ~ .),
    level = NULL
  ) +
  autolayer(
    total_test,
    Incidents
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Weekly EMS Demand: Actual vs. Forecast",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Incidents")
```

The total demand comparison shows which model family provides the most accurate forecasts for overall EMS volume. Evaluating both ARIMA and ETS on the same 52 week test period provides a more direct measure of forecasting performance than relying only on training set fit statistics.

## Life-Threatening vs. Non-Life-Threatening Demand

The final comparison evaluates ARIMA and ETS separately for each emergency category. This makes it possible to determine whether forecast accuracy differs between life threatening and non-life threatening EMS demand.

```{r}
category_fit <- category_train |>
  model(
    ARIMA = ARIMA(Incidents),
    ETS = ETS(Incidents))

category_fit
```

```{r}
category_fc <- category_fit |>
  forecast(new_data = category_test)

category_accuracy <- accuracy(category_fc, category_test) |>
  select(Category, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(Category, RMSE)

category_accuracy
```

```{r}
category_fc |>
  autoplot(
    category_train |> filter_index("2023 Jan" ~ .),
    level = NULL
  ) +
  autolayer(
    category_test,
    Incidents
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Category, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "EMS Demand Forecasts by Emergency Category",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Incidents")
```

### Forecasting Takeaways

The forecasting analysis evaluated three targets: total weekly EMS demand, life-threatening incidents, and non-life-threatening incidents. On the 52-week test set, ARIMA performed best for total demand (RMSE = 1,250; MAPE = 5.22%), while ETS performed best for life-threatening incidents (RMSE = 761; MAPE = 6.51%) and non-life-threatening incidents (RMSE = 715; MAPE = 5.61%) in the main model comparisons.

The initial non-life-threatening ARIMA comparison also showed that the manually selected ARIMA(0,1,1) model outperformed the automatically selected ARIMA model on the test set, demonstrating that a more complex model does not necessarily produce better forecasts.

Overall, no single model performed best across all forecasting targets. The results suggest that historical EMS data can provide useful estimates of future weekly demand, although forecasts remain subject to error. These findings could support staffing and resource planning by helping NYC EMS anticipate expected incident volumes while maintaining flexibility for unexpected changes.
